newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqi Kurds flee, Turkish Kurds vow to fight.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi Kurds flee, Turkish Kurds vow to fight.

text.p: Iraqi Kurds on Saturday fled their remote villages along the border in fear of a Turkish army incursion, but rebel Turkish Kurds vowed to exact a heavy toll from any invader.

"Every year the Turks raid our village. They cut down our fruit trees and bomb our houses, killing our livestock," said Khane Seini, as she left Banek, about 30 km (20 miles) east of the main border town of Zakho, on foot.
"The Turks and (President) Saddam Hussein both...kill us when they can. We need the United States to come and save us," said the 70-year-old widow, her belongings slung over her back.
Trailing not far behind was 13-year-old Azad Ali, leading two donkeys loaded down with bedding. "I am the last of my family out of the village. We are running because the Turks are coming."

Ankara announced on Thursday it was preparing to create a security zone just across the Iraqi border, five to 10 km (three to six miles) deep, to root out Turkish Kurdish guerrilla bases used to attack Turkish targets. So far it has yet to move in.
The United States has given conditional approval to the plan, but a number of other countries, among them France and Russia, have protested against the plan.

Every since the West created a safe haven in northern Iraq to protect Iraqi Kurds from the wrath of Saddam Hussein after the 1991 Gulf war, Turkey has mounted periodic incursions against its own rebels of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK).
Those operations left Iraqi Kurds, already under pressure fom Baghdad, trapped in a cross-fire.

In March of 1995, 35,000 Turkish troops backed by armour and air power pushed 40 km (25 miles) into northern Iraq in pursuit of PKK fighters, fighting for self-rule in southeast Turkey. The operation sent many Iraqi Kurds running for cover and drew widespread western condemnation.
"We can't afford to stay behind like we did last time," said Ali. "They killed one of my cousins and wounded several other villagers. They shelled the village then. We can't stand that situation."
Whole families shuttled back and forth between their mountain villages and the valleys to the south, outside the proposed security zone, hauling personal belongings and driving livestock to safety.
"The crops are ripe but we are leaving them and the fruit trees, too," said 55-year-old Nasir Sedak, as he walked outside Banek with his brother Said.
"We are walking now to hire vehicles to carry our belongings out. We will be gone by tonight or tomorrow morning," he said.
The villagers were quick to blame the presence of PKK forces for their plight, and Turkish Kurdish rebels were easy to find in many areas along the border.
"They bring trouble on their heels. If they were not here we would not have these problems," complained 27-year-old Bazad.
"There is no possibility they will leave unless the Turks drive them out, but that means we will be driven out as well."
Up one valley toward the Turkish border, beyond a checkpoint manned by three PKK fighters, a rebel divisonal commander granted reporters a brief interview.
Dostvan, 28, told reporters he was more worried about the recent upsurge in fighting between rival Iraqi Kurdish factions than he was about the possible arrival of the Turkish army.
"The (Kurd-on-Kurd) fighting that is taking place in the northern part of Iraq...we want to stop immediately. It is not in the interests of the Kurdish people," the commander said.
"If the Turks come we will launch a guerrilla war against them...We actually want them to come so we can deal them a heavy blow and defeat them."
Dostvan refused to disclose the size of his PKK force, sheltering behind a nearby hill. Villagers put the number at several hundred.
"It's true the PKK do not interfere with our business but that is nothing compared to the danger they bring us by just being there," said one woman in the area.
"We are exposed to shelling and bombing beacause of them," she said.
